waves.title: The UK data centre pipeline: what is actually building
waves.keywords: uk data centre pipeline, data centres under construction uk, uk data centre capacity MW, new data centres uk 2026, uk data centre planning approvals
waves.brief:
Reader: a developer, operator, land agent, consultant or contractor trying to size the real opportunity, deciding whether to commit bid resource, land or capital to UK schemes over the next 24 months. Their decision is which of the announced gigawatts will become buildings.

What ranks now: datacenterdynamics.com and datacentreknowledge.com news items on single projects, agency PDFs behind forms (Savills, Knight Frank, CBRE), and consultancy market-size pages. None gives a single UK page separating live, under construction, committed and speculative, and the agency research is gated so it never ranks. That gap is the article.

Structure: (1) the headline number and why it is wrong, (2) a table of the four tiers, (3) the three gates a scheme must pass (planning, grid, pre-let), (4) what the 2026 decisions tell you, (5) what to watch in 2027.

SOURCE ANCHORS (verified on the live web 17 November 2026; each must be attributed in the same sentence as the figure): Savills, in research published 11 June 2026, put UK live capacity at 1,803MW, of which it says London holds 1,637MW, about 91 per cent, up from 81 per cent in 2016; Savills put 242MW under construction with only about 66MW of that completing between Q2 and Q4 2026, UK vacancy at 8 per cent in Q1 2026 against 27 per cent in 2016, Q1 2026 take-up at 19MW against a record 217MW across 2025, and delivery at 231MW in 2025 and 48MW in Q1 2026. Savills' wider committed figure of 2,084MW and early-stage figure of 9,371MW came via a secondary summary of its 2026 Spotlight: WRITER MUST OPEN THE SAVILLS SPOTLIGHT PDF AND CONFIRM BOTH BEFORE PUBLICATION, or cut them. DESNZ, in its consultation Accelerating electricity network connections for strategic demand issued 11 March 2026, says about 140 data centre projects holding roughly 50GW sit in the transmission queue, against a total transmission demand queue of 96GW at end June 2025 plus 29GW at distribution, and states that speculative activity is materially inflating the demand pipeline. Set the 50GW of requests against the 242MW Savills counts in the ground: that contrast is the story.

PLANNING DECISIONS TO CARRY: Gowling WLG, 20 March 2026, reports the Government conceded a serious logical error in EIA screening for the Iver hyperscale scheme on previously developed Green Belt land, refused twice by Buckinghamshire Council then granted on call-in, with permission expected to be quashed by consent. LocalGov, 11 June 2026, reports the Housing Minister granted permission on appeal for Tritax Big Box's data centre and BESS on a 20-acre Green Belt site at Manor Farm, Slough, citing clear need and unprecedented demand, with Slough Borough Council calling it speculative. FTB Chambers, 1 November 2023, records the Secretary of State dismissing the Slough Availability Zone hyperscale appeal, with Green Belt openness harm given substantial weight.

STRUCTURAL: use "UK data centre pipeline" in the first paragraph. The four-tier capacity breakdown must be a table (tier, MW, source, date). Link out to the DESNZ consultation page on gov.uk, the Savills research page, and the Planning Inspectorate decision for Manor Farm, Slough.

SCOPE LIMITS: UK data centres are Critical National Infrastructure. Nothing on site security arrangements, perimeters, access control, resilience of specific halls or anything beyond what a published planning document already shows. Every investment and capacity figure is someone's claim: name who announced it, date it, and where an operator announcement and an independent estimate disagree, print both and say they disagree.

waves.title: Grid queue reform and your data centre timeline
waves.keywords: data centre grid connection uk, grid connection queue reform, gate 2 connection offer, NESO connections reform data centres, data centre power connection date
waves.brief:
Reader: the developer, asset manager or consultant who holds a connection agreement or is about to apply, and the M&E and power contractors whose programme hangs off the energisation date. The decision: do they keep paying to progress a scheme whose connection date may move, and do they switch to distribution, a private wire or on-site generation instead.

What ranks now: law firm notes (Gowling WLG, CMS, Burges Salmon, HSF Kramer, Shepherd and Wedderburn) that are written for other lawyers and stop at the reform's structure, plus NESO's own documents, which are unreadable for a commercial reader. No page answers the operator's question in operator language: what date can I promise my customer. That is what this piece does.

Structure: (1) what the queue reform actually did, (2) a table of the Gate 2 milestone dates, (3) the three ways a data centre loses its position, (4) transmission versus distribution, (5) what to do now, in order.

SOURCE ANCHORS (verified 17 November 2026): DESNZ, consultation Accelerating electricity network connections for strategic demand, issued 11 March 2026, closing 15 April 2026, page last updated 28 October 2026, states a transmission demand queue of 96GW at end June 2025 with a further 29GW at distribution, a combined transmission and distribution queue of 889GW of which DESNZ attributes 737GW to generation, interconnection and storage, around 140 data centre projects at transmission totalling roughly 50GW citing NESO's Call for Input, and growth in the transmission demand queue of 460 per cent in six months. The same consultation's Annex D illustrates a 200MW AI data centre being advanced from 2033 to 2029 and a future 500MW AI Growth Zone taking a 2034 connection with capacity reserved in 2028: these are DESNZ illustrations, not offers, and must be labelled as such. Ofgem's published agreement on revising the G2tWQ timetable records that it approved a revised timetable on 3 June 2026 and that, at NESO's request of 25 September 2026, the Gate 2 Phase 1 transmission offer deadline moved from 30 September 2026 to 31 October 2026, with distribution Phase 1 at 30 November 2026 and Phase 2 at 31 March 2027. WRITER MUST RE-OPEN THE OFGEM DOCUMENT AND NESO'S CONNECTIONS REFORM PAGE ON THE DAY OF WRITING: these dates have already slipped twice. Gowling WLG's 2026 note makes the point that matters most commercially, that the reforms bite on transmission-connected data centres and not on distribution-connected ones.

STRUCTURAL: use "data centre grid connection" in the first paragraph. The milestone dates must be a table (milestone, network, deadline, source and date). Link out to Ofgem's connections reform pages, NESO's connections reform page and the DESNZ consultation on gov.uk.

SCOPE LIMITS: CNI rule applies. No detail on specific substations, feeders, switchgear arrangements or site resilience beyond what published planning and regulatory documents show, and nothing on security. Attribute every GW, MW and date to the body that published it, in the same sentence, and say plainly where announcement figures and independent estimates diverge.

waves.title: AI Growth Zones: what they actually change
waves.keywords: ai growth zones, ai growth zone uk, ai growth zone sites, ai growth zone data centre, ai growth zone electricity discount
waves.brief:
Reader: an operator, investor, planner or local authority officer deciding whether a site inside or near a designated zone is worth more than one outside it, and whether to put resource into a bid. The decision is whether designation is a genuine commercial advantage or a press release.

What ranks now: gov.uk press releases with no figures, law firm explainers (Baker McKenzie, Burges Salmon, Addleshaw Goddard) written for lawyers, and computerweekly.com and datacenterdynamics.com news hits. Several widely shared pages give conflicting counts and dates for designated zones. There is no single UK page that lists the zones, dates them, and then says, concretely, what a developer gets. That is the article.

Structure: (1) what a designation is in law and what it is not, (2) a table of the designated zones, (3) the three things designation actually buys, (4) what it does not fix, (5) how a site gets considered.

SOURCE ANCHORS (verified 17 November 2026): the Government's AI Growth Zones policy paper, published 13 November 2025, sets out illustrative electricity cost discounts for a 500MW data centre of 24 pounds per MWh in Scotland, 16 pounds in Cumbria and 14 pounds in the North East, two new connection mechanisms reallocating released capacity and reserving capacity at named connection points, AI Growth Zone projects qualifying for the Connections Accelerator Service, and an aim to cut NSIP consent timelines from 18 months to 12 (summarised by Baker McKenzie, 9 January 2026; WRITER MUST CITE THE GOV.UK POLICY PAPER ITSELF). DSIT's press release of 30 April 2025 says the expression of interest process drew more than 200 responses and that proposals should have at least 500MW of access to existing power connections, which DSIT describes as enough to power 2 million homes. A written ministerial statement of 29 January 2026 names Lanarkshire as the fifth zone after Oxfordshire, North Wales, South Wales and the North East. Data Centre Review, 29 January 2026, reports the Lanarkshire zone centred on DataVita's campus with CoreWeave, at 100MW of AI-ready capacity, and reports UK ministers announcing 8.2 billion pounds of private investment: that is the Government's and the parties' claim and must be written as such, with the point made that no independent verification of the 8.2 billion figure exists. Burges Salmon, 16 December 2025, records a 4.5 million pound fund for a national team of AI data centre planning experts and the NPPF consultation published that day.

STRUCTURAL: use "AI Growth Zones" in the first paragraph. The zone list must be a table (zone, designation date, lead site or operator, announced capacity, announced investment, who announced it). Link out to the gov.uk AI Growth Zones policy paper, the written ministerial statement on parliament.uk and the NPPF consultation.

SCOPE LIMITS: CNI rule applies, nothing on site security arrangements. Every investment, jobs and megawatt figure in this sector is routinely inflated at announcement: attribute each one to whoever announced it, in the same sentence, date it, and where the Government's figure and an independent estimate differ, print both and say they differ.

waves.title: How to win work on a UK data centre build
waves.keywords: how to win data centre work, data centre contracts uk, supply into data centre construction, data centre subcontractor prequalification, data centre M&E contractors uk
waves.brief:
Reader: an owner or commercial director at a construction, M&E, electrical, cooling, fire, fibre or civils firm, turnover 2 million to 200 million pounds, who can see the build-out in the news and cannot see a way in. The decision is who to approach, at what tier, and what they need in place before the call is worth making. This is the single most commercially valuable query in the sector and it is genuinely unserved.

What ranks now: nothing useful. Searches land on DCD and Data Center Knowledge news, on vendor blogs selling products, and on US-centric Data Center Frontier pieces about the American market. Trade construction titles (Construction Enquirer, The Construction Index) report awards but never explain the procurement route. No UK page maps the tiers and names who buys at each one.

Structure: (1) the money flow, from end user to operator to developer to main contractor to specialist packages, (2) a table of recent live UK awards showing who appointed whom and at what tier, (3) the four routes in (main contractor supply chain, M&E specialist, direct to operator framework, enabling and civils), (4) what actually gets you prequalified (certifications, references at scale, commissioning capability, labour availability), (5) where to find the work: Find a Tender, operator supplier portals, main contractor supply chain registration, planning portals read as an early-warning system.

SOURCE ANCHORS (verified 17 November 2026, each dated and attributed to its reporting source): McLaren Construction announced its appointment to the shell and core of the first 70MW building at Ada Infrastructure's Docklands campus in London, one of three buildings planned, reported for completion in mid-2028, with the contract value not disclosed. McLaren Construction also announced appointment with Phoenix ME on predevelopment of Corscale's 140MW campus at Iver, Buckinghamshire, a scheme Construction Enquirer reported on 3 June 2026 at a 1 billion pound campus value: note this was a pre-construction services agreement, not a build contract. Construction Enquirer reported on 23 July 2026 that Blackpool Council selected Hochtief Data Centre Partner UK as preferred concessionaire for the 250 million pound first phase of Silicon Sands beside Blackpool Airport, a 6MW data centre plus around 20,000 sq ft of office and research space on a 40-acre masterplan under a 250-year lease, beating EdgeSynergies and Deep Green Technologies, with signing expected from 1 October. Construction Enquirer reported on 17 July 2026 that John F Hunt won a 20 million pound enabling works package at a CyrusOne data centre. Mace Construct was reported in January 2026 as contractor for a 168MW UK portfolio for Pathfinder Clean Energy, value undisclosed. Glencar was reported in 2026 on schemes at Brent Cross and for Pure DC in north London. Writer should add two or three fresher awards from Construction Enquirer on the day of writing.

STRUCTURAL: use "how to win work on a data centre build" or a close variant in the first paragraph. The awards map must be a table (scheme, client, main contractor, package, tier, value or undisclosed, source and date). Link out to Find a Tender, the named contractors' supply chain registration pages and the relevant council planning portals.

SCOPE LIMITS: CNI rule applies absolutely here. Nothing about security scope, perimeter works, access control packages or vetting arrangements, and nothing beyond what a published planning document or a public award notice already shows. Where a value is undisclosed, say undisclosed rather than estimating, and attribute every figure to the title that reported it in the same sentence.
